problems.reason: Both sentences state that Sebecus was an extinct genus that lived in South America during the Paleogene/Eocene.
Sentence 1 places Sebecus in the Paleogene, while sentence 21 extends its range to the Late Miocene or Early Pliocene.
Sentence 11 says the type species was found in the Sarmiento Formation, whereas sentence 12 says the partial skull and jaw belong to the Paleocene Mealla Formation.
Sentence 18 states Sebecosuchia is polyphyletic, while sentence 19 places Sebecus in the order Sebecosuchia.
Sentence 21 gives a range from Paleocene to Mid Eocene, but sentence 23 cites Laventense deposits (~12 Ma) extending the range into the Neogene.

notes: - contradiction: "Sebecus is an extinct genus of terrestrial, carnivorous crocodylomorph that lived in South America during the Paleogene period." / "Fossils of Sebecus range from the Paleocene to the Mid Eocene, with possible records extending to the Late Miocene or Early Pliocene.": Sentence 1 places Sebecus in the Paleogene, while sentence 21 extends its range to the Late Miocene or Early Pliocene.

- contradiction: "Simpson described the type species S. icaeorhinus based on a fragmented skull and lower jaw discovered in the Sarmiento Formation." / "The rock layer containing a partial skull and jaw belongs to the Paleocene Mealla Formation.": Sentence 11 says the type species was found in the Sarmiento Formation, whereas sentence 12 says the partial skull and jaw belong to the Paleocene Mealla Formation.

- contradiction: "Sebecus has been placed in various positions within the group of metasuchian crocodyliforms, and recent phylogenetic analyses suggest Sebecosuchia is polyphyletic, with Sebecus forming a metasuchian clade distantly related to Notosuchia." / "Colbert placed Sebecus and the Cretaceous Baurusuchus in the order Sebecosuchia because both possessed high, deep snouts and ziphodont teeth.": Sentence 18 states Sebecosuchia is polyphyletic, while sentence 19 places Sebecus in the order Sebecosuchia.

- contradiction: "Fossils of Sebecus range from the Paleocene to the Mid Eocene, with possible records extending to the Late Miocene or Early Pliocene." / "The deposits date to the Laventense (about 12 million years old), extending the genus's temporal range in the Neogene by nearly 40 million years.": Sentence 21 gives a range from Paleocene to Mid Eocene, but sentence 23 cites Laventense deposits (~12 Ma) extending the range into the Neogene.
